source: High Country Fly Fishing Experts like Due South Outfitters

conditions.overall: Early June conditions in the NC High Country bring warming days but cold, clear water at elevation. Delayed Harvest seasons are transitioning to harvest-open status as of June 6, 2026, meaning regulation changes are in effect on key streams.

top_flies.name: Elk Hair Caddis
top_flies.note: Reliable early-season dry fly for stocked and wild trout on hatchery-supported and delayed harvest waters in early April through June.

top_flies.name: Parachute Adams
top_flies.note: Classic all-around dry fly that works well on freestone High Country streams; effective during mixed hatch conditions.

top_flies.name: Pheasant Tail Nymph
top_flies.note: Go-to subsurface pattern for trout holding in riffles and runs on streams like the Watauga River and New River tributaries.

top_flies.name: Hare's Ear Nymph
top_flies.note: Versatile nymph matching a wide range of aquatic invertebrates; fish deep in pools and along seams.

top_flies.name: Woolly Bugger
top_flies.note: Effective streamer for larger browns and rainbows on delayed harvest waters; strip slowly through deeper pools.

top_flies.name: Zebra Midge
top_flies.note: Small midge pattern for clear, low-water conditions; especially effective when fish are sipping in slow tailouts.

top_flies.name: San Juan Worm
top_flies.note: Highly effective attractor nymph for freshly stocked fish on hatchery-supported waters; fish under an indicator.

tactics: On Delayed Harvest water that opened to harvest on June 6, be aware that regulations shift — verify current rules at ncwildlife.org before fishing and adjust your approach accordingly.
High Country streams at 3,300–4,000 ft run colder than lower-elevation WNC water — trout metabolism is still ramping up, so slow your presentation and fish nymphs deep through pools.
Fish early morning when water temps are coolest and trout are most active near the surface; surface activity slows as midday warms the shallows.
On stocked waters, freshly stocked fish often hold in the first available deep pool below an access point — target these areas with a San Juan Worm or Hare's Ear under an indicator.
Use barbless hooks or pinch your barbs, especially on catch-and-release sections — it speeds up release and is required on many DH stretches.
On small Ashe and Avery County tributaries, keep a low profile and use a short-line nymphing approach; these pressured fish spook easily in clear, low summer flows.

If crowds are heavy on main-stem Delayed Harvest sections like the Watauga River near Boone, move upstream to lesser-pressured tributaries or the Valle Crucis DH section for better solitude and willing fish.

waters.name: Watauga River (Boone / Valle Crucis DH Sections)
waters.note: Two Delayed Harvest sections totaling 2.2 miles opened to harvest on June 6, 2026. Valle Crucis section upstream typically sees lower pressure — a good alternative if the Boone access points are crowded. Classic pool-riffle-run water; 5,032 fish stocked annually.

waters.name: Helton Creek
waters.note: Largest Delayed Harvest fishery in Ashe County at 8 miles; 7,500 fish stocked annually. DH season opens to harvest June 6. Fish the upper reaches toward the VA line for less pressure.

waters.name: Big Horse Creek
waters.note: Has both a Delayed Harvest section (SR 1324 Bridge downstream to North Fork New River) and a Hatchery Supported section on the same stream — know the boundary before wading. DH section opened to harvest June 6.

waters.name: North Fork New River
waters.note: 20-mile hatchery-supported corridor in Ashe County gives explorers plenty of water; part of the 22,911-fish Ashe County stocking program. Good option for anglers looking to spread out.

waters.name: North Toe River (Avery County)
waters.note: Two separately managed stocked sections near Newland stocked in March and May; most productive stocked water in Avery County by fish count with 5,170 fish annually. Lower section toward Mitchell County line is the most heavily stocked stretch.

waters.name: Linville River
waters.note: High-elevation Catawba headwaters in Avery County; cold, clear water holds trout well into summer at this elevation.

waters.name: Elk River (Avery County)
waters.note: Drains toward Tennessee; one of three key Avery County watersheds for trout. Fish the stocked sections early in the season before summer pressure builds.

waters.name: Davidson River
waters.note: Lower-elevation WNC hatchery-supported water off US-276; one of the most popular Opening Day destinations in the region. Crowds arrive before dawn on opening day — have flies rigged and ready.

waters.name: Wilson Creek
waters.note: Western NC hatchery-supported stream included in Opening Day stocking; known for strong early-season fishing in April.

waters.name: Tuckasegee River
waters.note: One of four key WNC hatchery-supported Opening Day streams; good access and consistent stocking make it a reliable early-season destination.

waters.name: Nantahala River
waters.note: WNC hatchery-supported Opening Day stream; cold tailwater character keeps water temps stable through early summer.

elevation_note: High Country streams near Boone (3,300–4,000 ft) run 1-2 weeks behind lower-elevation WNC — hatches, water temps, and fish activity all lag behind what anglers may be seeing on lower-elevation rivers like the Davidson or Tuckasegee.
stocking_note: Watauga County Delayed Harvest streams received 5,032 fish stocked annually on the Watauga River; Ashe County stocked 22,911 fish across 15 waters in 2026; Avery County stocked 10,709 fish across 8 waters with stocking events in March and May 2026. Hatchery Supported waters on the Davidson, Tuckasegee, Nantahala, and Wilson Creek were stocked prior to April 4 Opening Day. Avery County North Toe River most recently stocked in May 2026.
